interest: This document provides valuable insight into the internal economic and administrative debates within the U.S. government during the implementation of the 'Dodge Line' in occupied Japan. It reveals high-level State Department consideration of shifting SCAP's military occupation toward a civilian model akin to the Allied High Commission in Germany, reflecting concerns over Japanese goodwill and international trade relations prior to a formal peace treaty. Furthermore, McDiarmid's technical commentary on Dodge's memorandum highlights nuanced economic disagreements between Washington financial specialists and Dodge over the inflationary mechanics of counterpart fund investments, while linking Japanese stabilization efforts directly to broader Cold War diplomacy, including the Council of Foreign Ministers negotiations in Paris over Germany and Austria.
overview: This file consists of a two-page letter dated June 22, 1949, from Orville J. McDiarmid, Associate Chief of the State Department's Division of Financial Affairs, to Joseph M. Dodge, President of The Detroit Bank and primary architect of the Dodge Line economic stabilization program for occupied Japan. Writing following Dodge's consultation visit to Washington, McDiarmid discusses the restructuring of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) occupation administration—suggesting that a civilian authority modeled on the German High Commission might grant greater autonomy to Japan without awaiting a formal peace treaty—and notes foreign trade obstacles such as British Commonwealth resistance. McDiarmid also offers a technical critique of Dodge's memorandum on counterpart fund financing and inflation, summarizes his work supporting the Council of Foreign Ministers (CFM) meeting in Paris concerning German currency and the Austrian state treaty, and encloses his recent article from the Far Eastern Survey on the Japanese exchange rate.

subfiles.summary: McDiarmid commends Dodge's 'Comments on the Inflation Problem' and discusses reorganizing SCAP along the lines of the German High Commission to grant greater responsibility to the Japanese government while preserving Allied policy objectives. He addresses the counterpart fund, clarifying that investments financed through aid-goods sales or tax revenues do not necessarily expand the money supply or fuel inflation in the manner Dodge suggested, though he concurs that a conservative approach remains prudent. McDiarmid also details his recent work backstopping the Council of Foreign Ministers in Paris regarding German currency and the Austrian treaty settlement, and encloses his published article from the Far Eastern Survey on the Japanese exchange rate problem.
